et horn.explanation: "Et horn" means "a horn". When you mean the musical instrument, it is also "et horn": "Han blæser i et jagthorn" (He blows a hunting horn). A deer has "et gevir" (a set of antlers), not horns: "Hjorten har et stort gevir" (The deer has big antlers).

et hospital.explanation: "Et hospital" means "a hospital". To say where you are, Danish uses "på" (on) where English says "at": "Jeg er på hospitalet" (I am at the hospital).

et hotel.explanation: "Et hotel" means "a hotel". To say where you are staying, Danish uses "på" (on) where English says "at": "Vi bor på hotel" (We are staying at a hotel).

et hotelværelse.explanation: "Et hotelværelse" means "a hotel room". It is built from hotel (hotel) and værelse (room). To say you have a booking: "Jeg har bestilt et hotelværelse" (I have booked a hotel room).

et hoved.explanation: "Et hoved" means "a head". To say your head hurts, Danish says "the head" where English says "my head": "Jeg har ondt i hovedet" (My head hurts, literally "I have a pain in the head"). In "hovedpine" (headache) it means the body part. In "hovedstad" (capital city) it means "main".

et hovedkvarter.explanation: "Et hovedkvarter" means "a headquarters". It is built from hoved (main) and et kvarter (a district).

et hul.explanation: "Et hul" means "a hole". To say you have a cavity, use it with "tanden" (the tooth): "Jeg har et hul i tanden" (I have a cavity in my tooth).

et humør.explanation: "Et humør" means "a mood". To say someone is in a bad mood, put "i" (in) before it: "Han er i dårligt humør" (He is in a bad mood).

et hundehalsbånd.explanation: "Et hundehalsbånd" means "a dog collar". It is built from hund (dog), hals (neck) and bånd (band).

et hus.explanation: "Et hus" means "a house". Do not mix it up with "et hjem" (a home). To talk about the building you buy, use "et hus": "Vi køber et hus" (We are buying a house). To talk about where you belong, use "et hjem": "Jeg savner mit hjem" (I miss my home).

et husdyr.explanation: "Et husdyr" means "a domestic animal". It is built from hus (house) and dyr (animal).

et husnummer.explanation: "Et husnummer" means "a house number". It is built from hus (house) and nummer (number). To write an address, put the number after the street name: "Nørregade 12" (Nørregade number 12).

et håndarbejde.explanation: "Et håndarbejde" means "a handicraft". It is built from hånd (hand) and arbejde (work). Do not mix it up with "et håndværk" (a skilled trade). To say someone works in a trade: "Min onkel er tømrer, og det er et håndværk" (My uncle is a carpenter, and that is a skilled trade).

et håndjern.explanation: "Et håndjern" means "a handcuff". It is built from hånd (hand) and jern (iron). To say someone is wearing handcuffs: "Han har håndjern på" (He has handcuffs on).

et håndklæde.explanation: "Et håndklæde" means "a towel". Do not mix it up with "et viskestykke" (a dish towel). To dry a dish, use "et viskestykke": "Jeg tørrer glasset med et viskestykke" (I dry the glass with a dish towel).

et håndled.explanation: "Et håndled" means "a wrist". It is built from en hånd (a hand) and et led (a joint). To say your wrist hurts: "Jeg har ondt i håndleddet" (My wrist hurts).

et håndtag.explanation: "Et håndtag" means "a handle". It is built from en hånd (a hand) and et tag (a hold), so it is what you take hold of.

et håndtryk.explanation: "Et håndtryk" means "a handshake". It is built from hånd (hand) and et tryk (a press). To say two people shake hands, use "at give hånd" (to shake hands): "Vi giver hinanden hånd" (We shake hands).

et håndværk.explanation: "Et håndværk" means "a craft". It is built from hånd (hand) and et værk (a work). Do not mix it up with "et håndarbejde" (a handicraft). To say what knitting is: "Hun strikker, og det er et håndarbejde" (She knits, and that is a handicraft).

et hårspænde.explanation: "Et hårspænde" means "a hair clip". It is built from hår (hair) and et spænde (a clasp).

et hæfte.explanation: "Et hæfte" means "a notebook". When you mean a thin booklet that comes with something, it is also "et hæfte": "et hæfte med opskrifter" (a booklet of recipes).

et højhus.explanation: "Et højhus" means "a high-rise". It is built from høj (tall) and hus (house).

et højskoleophold.explanation: "Et højskoleophold" means "a folk high school stay". It is built from "en højskole" (a folk high school) and "et ophold" (a stay). Folk high schools began in Denmark as schools where adults live and study together.

et høreapparat.explanation: "Et høreapparat" means "a hearing aid". It is built from høre (hear) and et apparat (a device).

had.explanation: "Had" means "a hatred". It is the noun for the verb "at hade" (to hate). To say who the hatred is aimed at, add "mod" (toward): "Hun følte had mod ham" (She felt hatred toward him).

hagl.explanation: "Hagl" means "hail". When you mean the small lead pellets fired from a shotgun, it is also "hagl": "Jægeren lader sit haglgevær med hagl" (The hunter loads his shotgun with pellets).

hakket oksekød.explanation: "Hakket oksekød" means "ground beef". It is built from hakket (chopped) and oksekød (beef). To say ground pork, swap the meat: "hakket svinekød" (ground pork).

hallo.explanation: "Hallo" means "hello". To get someone's attention, say it sharply: "Hallo, hører du efter?" (Hello, are you listening?).

halløj.explanation: "Halløj" means "hey". It is an informal greeting. To greet a friend and ask how things are: "Halløj, hvad så?" (Hey, what is up?).

halm.explanation: "Halm" means "straw". Do not mix it up with "et sugerør" (a drinking straw). To say you drink through a straw: "Jeg drikker med et sugerør" (I drink with a drinking straw).

halv.explanation: "Halv" means "half". It goes before the word it describes: "en halv liter" (half a liter). To say half past the hour on the clock, count toward the next hour: "klokken fire" (four o'clock) is 4:00, but "halv fire" is 3:30, half an hour before four.

halv tre.explanation: "Halv tre" means "half past two". Danish counts halfway toward the next hour, so 2:30 is "halv tre" (halfway to three).

halvanden.explanation: "Halvanden" means "one and a half". To say an hour and a half, put it before "time" (hour): "halvanden time". Before "år" (year) it changes to "halvandet": "halvandet år" (a year and a half).

halvdelen.explanation: "Halvdelen" means "a half". To name the whole that the half comes from, add "af" (of): "halvdelen af pengene" (half of the money). For a measure such as half a liter, use "halv" (half): "en halv liter" (half a liter).

halvvejs.explanation: "Halvvejs" means "halfway". It is built from halv (half) and vej (way). To talk about time: "halvvejs gennem året" (halfway through the year).

ham.explanation: "Ham" means "him". When a man receives the action, use "ham": "Jeg hjælper ham" (I help him). When the man does the action, use "han" (he): "Han hjælper mig" (He helps me). After "med" (with) it is also "ham": "Jeg går med ham" (I am going with him).

han.explanation: "Han" means "he". When a man does the action, use "han": "Han hjælper mig" (He helps me). When the man receives the action, use "ham" (him): "Jeg hjælper ham" (I help him).

handsker.explanation: "Handsker" means "gloves". Do not mix it up with "en vante" (a mitten). To say children wear mittens: "Børnene har røde vanter på" (The children have red mittens on).

hans.explanation: "Hans" means "his". When the owner is a man other than the one doing the action, use "hans": "Peter vasker hans bil" (Peter washes another man's car). To say the man's own, use "sin": "Peter vasker sin bil" (Peter washes his own car).

hardware.explanation: "Hardware" means "hardware". Danish took this word from English and spells it the same way.

hav en god dag.explanation: "Hav en god dag" means "have a good day". To say it as a goodbye and get a reply: "Hav en god dag!" "Tak, i lige måde." (Have a good day! Thanks, you too.) To wish someone a good evening, swap "dag" (day) for "aften" (evening): "Hav en god aften" (Have a good evening).

havearbejde.explanation: "Havearbejde" means "gardening". It is built from have (garden) and arbejde (work). To say you do it, use "at lave" (to make): "Jeg laver havearbejde" (I do gardening).

havre.explanation: "Havre" means "oats". In "havregryn" (rolled oats) and "havremælk" (oat milk), "havre" is the first part of the word.

havregryn.explanation: "Havregryn" means "oatmeal". It is built from havre (oats) and gryn (groats). To name the cooked porridge, say "havregrød" (oatmeal porridge): "Jeg laver havregrød" (I am making oatmeal porridge).

havremælk.explanation: "Havremælk" means "oat milk". It is built from havre (oats) and mælk (milk).

hed.explanation: "Hed" means "hot". Do not mix it up with "varm" (warm), which is milder: "Vandet er varmt" (The water is warm). When the thing described takes "et", add "t": "et hedt bad" (a hot bath).

hej.explanation: "Hej" means "hi". To say goodbye, say it twice: "Hej hej!" (Bye bye!).

hej med dig.explanation: "Hej med dig" means "hi there". When you leave, it also means "bye": "Hej med dig, vi ses!" (Bye, see you!). To greet several people, say "hej med jer" (hi to you all): "Hej med jer!" (Hi to you all!).

hejsa.explanation: "Hejsa" means "hi there". It is an informal, cheerful version of "hej" (hi). To greet someone and ask how they are: "Hejsa, hvordan har du det?" (Hi there, how are you?).

hektisk.explanation: "Hektisk" means "hectic". Before a word that takes "et", it does not add "t": "et hektisk liv" (a hectic life). With several things, it adds "e": "hektiske tider" (hectic times).

hel.explanation: "Hel" means "whole". To say a whole thing, put it before the noun: "en hel kage" (a whole cake). Before a word that takes "et", add "t": "et helt æble" (a whole apple). To say "the whole day", use "hele": "hele dagen" (the whole day). When something is not broken, it also means "unbroken": "Koppen er hel" (The cup is unbroken).

helbred.explanation: "Helbred" means "health". To say someone's health is poor, put "dårligt" (poor) before it: "Han har dårligt helbred" (He has poor health). Do not mix it up with "sund" (healthy), which describes food: "sund mad" (healthy food).

held.explanation: "Held" means "luck". It is the first word in the phrase "held og lykke" (good luck): "Held og lykke med eksamen" (Good luck with the exam).

heldig.explanation: "Heldig" means "lucky". It comes from "held" (luck), as does "heldigvis" (fortunately). Before a word that takes "et", add "t": "et heldigt valg" (a lucky choice).

heldigvis.explanation: "Heldigvis" means "fortunately". To say you are glad about how something turned out: "Heldigvis er det fredag" (Fortunately it is Friday). The opposite is "desværre" (unfortunately): "Desværre har jeg ikke tid" (Unfortunately I do not have time).

hele tiden.explanation: "Hele tiden" means "all the time". Literally, it is "the whole time". To say "always", use "altid" (always): "Han kommer altid til tiden" (He always arrives on time).

heller.explanation: "Heller" means "either", as in "not either". To say yes to the same thing, use "også" (too): "Jeg kan også komme" (I can come too). To say no, use "heller ikke": "Jeg kan heller ikke komme" (I cannot come either).

hellere.explanation: "Hellere" means "rather". With "må" (must) it means "had better": "Du må hellere gå nu" (You had better go now). Do not mix it up with "heller" (either): "Jeg kan heller ikke komme" (I cannot come either).

hellere end.explanation: "Hellere end" means "rather than". To say which choice you take and which you skip, name the one you take first: "Jeg tager toget hellere end bilen" (I take the train rather than the car). To say "better late than never": "Hellere sent end aldrig" (literally, "rather late than never").

hellig.explanation: "Hellig" means "sacred". Before a word that takes "et", add "t": "et helligt sted" (a holy place). It is also the first part of "helligdag" (public holiday), literally "holy day".

helst.explanation: "Helst" means "preferably". To say what you would like most: "Jeg vil helst blive hjemme" (I would most like to stay home). To say you would rather not: "Skal du med?" "Helst ikke." (Are you coming? Preferably not.)

helt.explanation: "Helt" means "completely". To say something is complete, put it before the word: "Jeg er enig" (I agree) becomes "Jeg er helt enig" (I completely agree).

hemmelig.explanation: "Hemmelig" means "secret". Before a word that takes "et", add "t": "et hemmeligt sted" (a secret place). The noun is "en hemmelighed" (a secret): "Det er en hemmelighed" (It is a secret).

hemmelighedsfuld.explanation: "Hemmelighedsfuld" means "secretive". It is built from "en hemmelighed" (a secret) and "-fuld" (full of). The ending "-fuld" also appears in "hensynsfuld" (considerate). Before a word that takes "et", add "t": "et hemmelighedsfuldt smil" (a secretive smile).

hen.explanation: "Hen" means "over", as in moving over to a place. When someone moves to a place, use it with the verb: "Gå hen til døren" (Walk over to the door). For where someone already is, use "henne" (over there): "Han står henne ved døren" (He stands over there by the door).

hende.explanation: "Hende" means "her". When a woman receives the action, use "hende": "Jeg hjælper hende" (I help her). When the woman does the action, use "hun" (she): "Hun hjælper mig" (She helps me). After "med" (with) it is also "hende": "Jeg går med hende" (I am going with her).

hendes.explanation: "Hendes" means "her". When the owner is a woman other than the one doing the action, use "hendes": "Anna vasker hendes bil" (Anna washes another woman's car). To say the woman's own, use "sin": "Anna vasker sin bil" (Anna washes her own car).

hensynsfuld.explanation: "Hensynsfuld" means "considerate". It is built from "et hensyn" (a consideration) and "-fuld" (full of). Before a word that takes "et", add "t": "et hensynsfuldt svar" (a considerate answer).

her.explanation: "Her" means "here". To say where you are: "Jeg står her" (I am standing here). For a place away from you, use "der" (there): "Du står der" (You are standing there). Do not mix it up with the English word "her", which is "hende" in Danish: "Jeg ser hende" (I see her).

herfra.explanation: "Herfra" means "from here". It is built from her (here) and fra (from). For a place away from you, use "derfra" (from there): "Det er langt derfra" (It is far from there).

herhen.explanation: "Herhen" means "here", when someone moves toward the speaker. To say someone walks toward the speaker: "Hun går herhen" (She walks here). To say where someone already is, use "her" (here): "Jeg er her" (I am here).

herinde.explanation: "Herinde" means "in here". It is built from her (here) and inde (inside). When someone outside says where a person is, use "derinde" (in there): "Hun er derinde" (She is in there).

herlig.explanation: "Herlig" means "wonderful". Before a word that takes "et", add "t": "et herligt vejr" (lovely weather). With several things, it adds "e": "herlige børn" (lovely children).

hermed.explanation: "Hermed" means "hereby". It is built from her (here) and med (with). It is a formal word. To announce that something is now official: "Hermed erklæres mødet for åbnet" (The meeting is hereby declared open).

hertil.explanation: "Hertil" means "here", when someone moves toward the place. To add one more thing to what you just said: "Hertil kommer prisen" (On top of this comes the price).

herude.explanation: "Herude" means "out here". It is built from her (here) and ude (out). For a place away from you, use "derude" (out there): "Det er koldt derude" (It is cold out there).

hidsig.explanation: "Hidsig" means "hot-tempered". Before a word that takes "et", add "t": "et hidsigt temperament" (a hot temper). With several people, it adds "e": "hidsige drenge" (hot-tempered boys).

hidtil.explanation: "Hidtil" means "so far". To say things go on as before: "Vi gør det som hidtil" (We do it as before). For a set end point, use "indtil" (until): "Jeg bliver indtil fredag" (I am staying until Friday).

hinanden.explanation: "Hinanden" means "each other". To say people do the same thing to one another: "De vasker hinanden" (They wash each other). To say each person does it to themselves, use "sig" (themselves): "De vasker sig" (They wash themselves).

hinsides.explanation: "Hinsides" means "beyond", as in on the far side of a place: "hinsides floden" (beyond the river). To say something is past a limit, it also means "beyond": "hinsides enhver tvivl" (beyond any doubt).

historisk.explanation: "Historisk" means "historic". To say something is about the past, it means "historical": "en historisk roman" (a historical novel).

hittegods.explanation: "Hittegods" means "lost and found". It is built from "at hitte" (to find) and "gods" (goods). To say where you ask for lost things: "Hittegodset er åbent i dag" (The lost and found is open today).

hjem.explanation: "Hjem" means "home". When you are heading there, use it with a verb of moving: "Jeg går hjem" (I am going home). When you are already there, use "hjemme" (at home): "Jeg er hjemme" (I am at home).

hjemlig.explanation: "Hjemlig" means "homey". Before a word that takes "et", add "t": "et hjemligt køkken" (a homey kitchen). When you mean from your own country, it means "domestic": "hjemlige produkter" (domestic products).

hjemløs.explanation: "Hjemløs" means "homeless". It is built from hjem (home) and the ending -løs (without). To talk about the people, use it as a noun: "de hjemløse" (the homeless).

hjemme.explanation: "Hjemme" means "at home", where you already are: "Jeg er hjemme" (I am at home). When you are heading there, use "hjem" (home): "Jeg går hjem" (I am going home). To say at someone's place, add "hos" (at): "hjemme hos mig" (at my place).

hjemmelavet.explanation: "Hjemmelavet" means "homemade". It is built from hjemme (at home) and lavet (made). The word "lavet" (made) is also in "håndlavet" (handmade).

hjælp.explanation: "Hjælp" means "help". It takes "en" (hjælpen), but to ask for help in general, leave it out: "Kan jeg få hjælp?" (Can I get help?) To thank someone: "Tak for hjælpen" (Thanks for the help).

hjælpeløs.explanation: "Hjælpeløs" means "helpless". It is built from hjælp (help) and the ending -løs (without). To say how you feel: "Jeg følte mig hjælpeløs" (I felt helpless). Do not confuse it with "hjælpsom" (helpful): "en hjælpsom nabo" (a helpful neighbor).

hjælpsom.explanation: "Hjælpsom" means "helpful". Before a word that takes "et", add "t": "et hjælpsomt barn" (a helpful child). Do not mix it up with "hjælpeløs" (helpless): "en hjælpeløs baby" (a helpless baby).

hjælpsomhed.explanation: "Hjælpsomhed" means "helpfulness". It is built from "hjælpsom" (helpful) and the ending -hed (-ness). To thank someone: "Tak for din hjælpsomhed" (Thanks for your helpfulness).

hold da op.explanation: "Hold da op" means "wow". To react to something impressive: "Hold da op, hvor flot!" (Wow, how pretty!) Do not mix it up with "hold op" (stop it): "Hold op med det!" (Stop that!).

hold kæft.explanation: "Hold kæft" means "shut up". It is rude. When you are very surprised, it can also mean "wow": "Hold kæft, hvor er det flot!" (Wow, that is so pretty!)

hold op.explanation: "Hold op" means "stop it". To say you stop doing something, add "med at" (literally, "with to") before the verb: "Jeg holder op med at ryge" (I am quitting smoking).

holdbar.explanation: "Holdbar" means "lasting". When you talk about a material, it means "durable": "et holdbart materiale" (a durable material). It is also the first part of "holdbarhedsdato" (best-before date).

holland.explanation: "Holland" means "the Netherlands". Danish has no word for "the" before it: "Jeg bor i Holland" (I live in the Netherlands).
